question: To trim the elevator in a nose-up (trailing edge up) position, the elevator trim tab deflects:

options.text: Down
Up
In the same direction as the elevator
Neutral

explanation: The tab's upward force behind the hinge holds the elevator trailing edge up with zero stick force. A trim tab always deflects opposite to the surface it trims.

question: A trim tab removes stick force by:

options.text: Producing a hinge moment that holds the surface at the required deflection
Changing the aircraft's CG, which moves the balance point of the whole aircraft so that the elevator no longer needs to be held against the control column
Changing the aircraft's CG
Increasing control power

explanation: The tab alters only the hinge moment balance; the pitching moment is still produced by the deflected elevator.

question: Trimming with an elevator tab reduces the remaining elevator travel available:

options.text: Only in the opposite direction
In neither direction, because a tab trim setting is independent of the surface deflection and so the remaining travel stays the same whatever the trim
In the direction the elevator is already deflected
In both directions equally

explanation: A tab trims by holding the elevator deflected; that deflection is taken from its travel range. A trimmable stabiliser avoids this.

question: A ground-adjustable (fixed) tab is used to:

options.text: Correct a permanent out-of-trim tendency found in flight test, such as a wing heaviness
Balance the elevator in turbulence
Act as a servo tab
Trim in flight, since the fixed tab can be adjusted by the pilot from the cockpit at any time and so replaces the trim wheel for every normal flight

explanation: Bent on the ground to a set angle, it removes a constant hinge moment at a typical cruise condition.

question: When the pilot selects nose-up trim, the stick force needed to hold a nose-up attitude:

options.text: Is unchanged
Falls toward zero, because the tab now holds the elevator
Increases, because the tab is now working against the elevator and so the pilot must hold the column harder to keep the nose up in every case
Reverses permanently at every speed

explanation: Trim re-centres the zero-force condition at the new elevator angle.

question: An adjustable (trimmable) horizontal stabiliser trims the aircraft by:

options.text: Changing the tailplane incidence so the elevator can be faired at zero stick force
Changing wing incidence
Deflecting a tab on the elevator
Deflecting a tab on the elevator, which holds the surface at the trimmed angle and removes the pilot's need to hold any force on the control column at all

explanation: The whole stabiliser produces the trim load; the elevator stays near neutral with its full travel available.

question: Compared with tab trim, a trimmable stabiliser is preferred on large, high-speed aircraft because:

options.text: It needs no actuator
It reduces the CG range
It provides large trim forces over a wide CG and speed range while keeping full elevator authority and lower trim drag
It reduces the CG range, since the stabiliser moves the centre of gravity to a fixed position and so the aircraft is always flown at a single balance point

explanation: Large trim changes (flap, Mach, CG) would consume most elevator travel if trimmed by tab; the faired elevator also reduces drag.

question: At take-off, the stabiliser trim is set according to CG position because:

options.text: Trim changes the stall speed
Trim affects V1, because the stabiliser setting changes the take-off decision speed directly and so must be set to match the speed chosen for the take-off
Rotation force and pitch response depend on the CG; a forward CG needs more nose-up trim
Trim is only for cruise

explanation: A forward CG needs a larger tail download to rotate. Correct setting gives normal rotation force; a mis-set can make rotation heavy or premature.

question: A runaway stabiliser trim is dangerous because:

options.text: The stabiliser is more powerful than the elevator and can produce forces the elevator cannot counter at high q
It only affects roll, since the stabiliser moves the aircraft about the lateral axis only and the pitch response is unaffected in every flight condition
It is self-correcting
It reduces the stall speed

explanation: Tail force from stabiliser incidence acts on the whole surface; elevator authority to oppose it is limited and diminishes as the mistrim grows.

question: For a statically stable aircraft trimmed at a given speed, a speed increase with no change in trim requires:

options.text: A push force, and releasing it returns the aircraft toward the trim speed
A pull force
A pull force, because a faster aircraft in a stable trim condition always tends to pitch up and so the pilot must pull to hold the attitude constant
A push force, and the aircraft then accelerates further

explanation: Positive speed stability: above trim speed the aircraft pitches up; the pilot must push to hold the higher speed.

question: Trimming for a new speed changes:

options.text: The speed at which stick force is zero, not the aircraft's basic stability
The CG position, which is changed by the trim wheel and so the trim setting for a new speed always moves the balance point of the aircraft
The neutral point
The static margin

explanation: Trim moves the zero-force point along the force–speed line; the gradient reflects stability, which trim does not alter.

question: A trimmed aircraft is disturbed nose-down, gains speed and is left alone (stick free). It will:

options.text: Continue to accelerate
Remain at the new speed
Pitch up and oscillate back toward the trim speed
Remain at the new speed, since a stable aircraft with the stick free holds whatever speed it reaches and does not return toward the trim speed on its own

explanation: Above trim speed the aircraft generates a nose-up tendency (stick-free speed stability) — the phugoid follows.

question: On an aircraft with engines below the CG, increasing thrust typically produces:

options.text: No pitch change
A nose-down pitch change
A nose-up pitch change requiring nose-down trim
A nose-down pitch change, because the extra thrust pulls the engines' line down and so the aircraft pitches down by an amount that is the same at every speed

explanation: Moment = T × vertical offset; engines below the CG rotate the nose up as thrust increases.

question: Moving the CG forward within limits requires:

options.text: More nose-down trim
No trim change, since the forward movement of the CG is balanced by the reduced tail load and so the aircraft holds the same trim setting throughout
Less tail download
More nose-up trim and a larger tail download

explanation: The wing lift's nose-down moment arm about the CG grows; the tail must produce more download.

question: Extending trailing-edge flaps usually requires a trim change because:

options.text: The wing moment and the tail downwash both change, altering pitch balance
The CG moves aft, since flap extension adds weight to the rear of the aircraft and so the centre of gravity shifts behind its normal position
Engine thrust rises
The fin area changes

explanation: C_M,ac becomes more negative and tail downwash increases; the net change depends on the configuration.

question: Burning fuel from a tank aft of the CG changes the trim requirement because:

options.text: The neutral point moves
The CG moves aft, requiring more nose-up trim
Only weight changes, since the fuel is removed and the balance point is unaffected by where it was stored in the aircraft at any stage of the flight
The CG moves forward, requiring more nose-up trim

explanation: Removing mass aft of the CG shifts the CG forward.

question: Trim drag is reduced when:

options.text: The CG moves forward, which reduces the trim load on the tail and so produces less trim drag at every speed the aircraft is able to fly
The tail trim load is reduced, e.g. by an aft CG within limits
The elevator is deflected with tab
The tail download increases

explanation: Less download means less wing lift to carry and less tail induced drag. Some aircraft move fuel aft in cruise for this reason.

question: Speed brakes increase drag. W = 600 kN, idle thrust 5 kN, drag 40 kN. Deploying speed brakes adds 20 kN. The descent angle at constant speed changes from:
With speed brakes extended at 280 kt TAS in the previous example (sin γ = 0.092), the rate of descent is about:

options.text: 26,000 ft/min
1,600 ft/min
2,600 ft/min
260 ft/min

question: Flight spoilers used as speed brakes reduce CLmax by 10 %. The stall speed rises by:
Speed brakes allow a steeper descent without increasing speed because:

options.text: They increase lift, which lets the aircraft hold a higher speed in the descent and so the descent path is steepened without any change in the rate of descent
They increase thrust
They increase drag, so a larger weight component along the path is needed to balance it at the same speed
They reduce weight

explanation: At constant speed D − T = W·sin γ; more drag → larger γ.

question: Lift dumpers (ground spoilers) are designed to:

options.text: Reduce drag on landing, since the dumpers add a large amount of drag to the aircraft as it rolls and so shorten the distance needed to stop on the runway
Destroy wing lift after touchdown so weight transfers to the wheels for braking
Provide roll control in cruise only
Increase lift for take-off

explanation: Wheel braking force = μ(W − L); dumping lift raises the normal force and adds aerodynamic drag.

question: Deploying upper-surface spoilers symmetrically in flight typically produces:

options.text: A lift increase
A drag increase, a lift decrease at constant α, and a pitch change that may need trim
A roll only, since symmetric deflection of the spoilers acts on both wings equally and so removes any rolling tendency that the surfaces might otherwise give
No pitch change on any aircraft

explanation: Spoilers alter the wing's lift and pitching moment and the downwash at the tail; the resulting pitch change depends on geometry.

question: Spoiler panels used for roll control are raised on:

options.text: The up-going wing
Neither wing in flight
Both wings equally
The down-going wing

explanation: Spoiling lift on the wing that should descend produces the roll and proverse yaw.

question: Speed brakes are generally not used below a certain height on approach because:

options.text: They raise the stall speed and sink rate and reduce the margin available for recovery
They increase lift
They increase lift, which keeps the aircraft flying at a speed above the stall and so makes the speed brakes safe to use at any height on the approach
They are ineffective at low speed

explanation: Lower CLmax and higher drag reduce energy margin close to the ground.

question: A fuel imbalance of 1,000 kg at 6 m from the centreline produces a rolling moment of:

options.text: 5.9 kN·m
589 kN·m
6.0 kN·m

explanation: M = m·g·d = 1,000 × 9.81 × 6 = 58,860 N·m. Aileron trim (or fuel transfer) removes it.

question: After an engine failure on a twin, rudder trim is used to:

options.text: Lower the minimum control speed
Increase the yawing moment, since the trim tab is set to add to the asymmetric force and so the pilot can fly with a lighter rudder at all speeds
Remove the sustained rudder pedal force needed to balance the asymmetric yawing moment
Replace the need for rudder authority

explanation: Trim holds the rudder deflection with zero pedal force; it does not add authority beyond full rudder.

question: Aileron trim in a light aircraft is often a ground-adjustable tab because:

options.text: Ailerons cannot be trimmed in flight, since the lateral control surfaces are locked by the aileron balance system whenever the aircraft is airborne at any speed
Ailerons cannot be trimmed in flight
Lateral out-of-trim is small and nearly constant, arising from rigging and asymmetry
Roll trim changes with speed squared only

explanation: A fixed correction is sufficient where lateral trim changes are small in flight.

question: A yaw from propeller effects at high power and low speed in a single-engine aircraft is best removed by:

options.text: Flap extension
Aileron trim, which rolls the aircraft back toward the level position and so removes any yaw from the propeller, since the two effects are linked at all power settings
Rudder trim (where fitted) or an offset fin/engine thrust line
Elevator trim

explanation: Slipstream and asymmetric blade effects produce a yawing moment that varies with power and speed; rudder trim cancels the residual.

question: Mach trim systems compensate for:

options.text: The pitch-up at low speed
Adverse yaw, since the Mach trim system works on the lateral axis and removes any yawing moment that arises as the aircraft accelerates in the transonic range
Roll due to fuel imbalance
The nose-down pitch (tuck under) caused by aft movement of the centre of pressure at high Mach

explanation: As shock waves form, the wing CP moves aft and tail downwash changes; Mach trim applies nose-up trim or elevator automatically with Mach number.

question: Without a functioning Mach trim, an aircraft at high Mach number will:

options.text: Develop a nose-down tendency with increasing speed, requiring increasing pull force
Have no pitch change
Pitch up with increasing speed
Have no pitch change, because the centre of pressure stays in the same place at all Mach numbers and so the aircraft holds its attitude at every speed

explanation: Tuck under is a speed-unstable pitch characteristic; limitations usually reduce the permitted Mach number when the system is inoperative.

question: Trimmed at 200 kt, the aircraft slows to 180 kt without re-trimming. The pilot must:

options.text: Push
Pull to hold the lower speed
Apply no force
Pull at higher speed, push at lower speed

explanation: Below trim speed a stable aircraft tends to pitch down to regain the trim speed; holding the lower speed needs a pull.

question: A trimmable stabiliser is typically driven by:

options.text: Aerodynamic floating
A jackscrew actuator that holds position under load (irreversible)
A servo tab, which moves the stabiliser through a linkage and so holds it in position without any load being carried by the jackscrew at all
A spring tab

explanation: The screw jack resists back-driving by the large tail loads, keeping the set incidence.

question: On a servo-tab-operated elevator, trimming is achieved by:

options.text: Moving the stabiliser, since the servo tab's neutral position is linked to the stabiliser's own angle and so a change of stabiliser setting always alters the elevator trim
Moving the stabiliser
Offsetting the neutral position of the servo tab
Deflecting the elevator directly

explanation: Changing the tab's datum sets the elevator's floating position for zero pilot force.

question: Landing-gear extension commonly produces a nose-down pitch change, caused mainly by:

options.text: The gear's weight moving aft
Thrust increase
Thrust increase, since the gear is extended at the moment the power is raised and the extra thrust always pitches the nose down by a fixed amount
The drag of the gear acting below the CG

explanation: Drag below the CG produces a nose-down moment; gear extension also shifts mass forward or aft depending on retraction direction.

question: Speed brakes that increase drag without changing lift distribution significantly are typically located:

options.text: On the fuselage or as split surfaces at the tail
On the ailerons
On the ailerons, which are mounted on the outer wing and so change the lift distribution along the span in a way that is consistent with the wing's own stall pattern
As spoilers on the outer wing

explanation: Fuselage or tail-cone brakes add drag near the CG line with little effect on lift or roll.

question: The trim change on selecting a large power reduction in a propeller aircraft with engines above the CG line is:

options.text: A roll
Nose-up
Nose-down
None

explanation: Thrust above the CG gives a nose-down moment; reducing it removes that moment, pitching the nose up. Slipstream over the tail modifies the result.

question: The aim of trimming is:

options.text: To reduce the control force to zero at the desired flight condition
To increase control authority
To increase control authority, since trimming adds deflection to every control surface and so the aircraft can be flown further from its balance point in both directions
To move the neutral point

explanation: Trim is a hinge-moment or incidence adjustment for zero force; stability and authority are set elsewhere.

question: Trimming the stabiliser nose-up means:

options.text: Its leading edge moves down, increasing the tailplane's negative incidence and download
Its leading edge moves up
Its leading edge moves up, which reduces the tailplane's negative incidence and so lowers the download on the tail at every speed the aircraft can attain
The elevator deflects down

explanation: More negative incidence increases the download, pitching the nose up.

question: An aircraft trimmed in cruise is slowed by 20 % at constant altitude. With a trimmable stabiliser, the trim change needed is:

options.text: Nose-up, to increase the tail download for the higher α and CL
Only rudder trim
Only rudder trim, since a slower aircraft with a trimmable stabiliser needs no change in the tail setting and so only the yaw trim must be altered in cruise
Nose-down

explanation: Lower speed needs a higher CL (×1.56) and α; the tail must hold the new α — a nose-up trim input in a stable aircraft.
